questions.question: Why is clock synchronization difficult in distributed systems?

options.text: Network delays are variable and unpredictable, making it impossible to know exact message transit time
All computers use the same clock
Clocks don't exist in distributed systems

questions.explanation: Network latency varies unpredictably. When Node A sends its time to Node B, B doesn't know how long the message took. This uncertainty makes perfect synchronization impossible—we can only bound the error.

questions.question: What is clock drift?

options.text: The gradual divergence of a clock from true time due to hardware imperfections

questions.explanation: Crystal oscillators in computers aren't perfect. A typical drift rate is 10-100 ppm (parts per million), meaning clocks can drift apart by seconds per day. Without synchronization, clocks diverge over time.

questions.question: What is NTP (Network Time Protocol) used for?

options.text: Synchronizing clocks across computers over a network

questions.explanation: NTP synchronizes clocks to UTC using a hierarchy of time servers. It accounts for network delay by measuring round-trip time. Typical accuracy: milliseconds over internet, microseconds on LAN.

questions.question: What is the NTP stratum hierarchy?

options.text: Layers of time servers where Stratum 0 are atomic clocks, Stratum 1 directly connected to them, and so on

questions.explanation: Stratum 0: atomic clocks, GPS. Stratum 1: servers directly connected to Stratum 0. Stratum 2: sync to Stratum 1, etc. Each level adds potential error. Most computers sync to Stratum 2-3 servers.

questions.question: What problem can occur if a system clock jumps backward?

options.text: Log timestamps become non-monotonic, cache TTLs break, unique ID generation can produce duplicates

questions.explanation: Backward clock jumps cause: duplicate timestamps in logs, cache entries expiring early or late, time-based UUIDs colliding, scheduled tasks running twice. Many systems assume monotonic time.

questions.question: What is Google's TrueTime API designed to provide?

options.text: Bounded clock uncertainty with explicit error intervals

questions.explanation: TrueTime returns an interval [earliest, latest] guaranteed to contain the true time. Spanner uses this to implement external consistency—it waits out the uncertainty before committing. Requires GPS and atomic clocks.

questions.question: How does Cristian's algorithm estimate clock offset?

options.text: By measuring round-trip time and assuming symmetric network delay

questions.explanation: Client sends request at T1, server responds with its time Ts, client receives at T4. Estimated offset = Ts - (T1 + RTT/2). Assumes request and response take equal time—not always true.

questions.question: What is the Berkeley Algorithm for clock synchronization?

options.text: A master polls all clocks, computes average, and tells each node how to adjust
Only the fastest clock is used

questions.explanation: Berkeley Algorithm: master polls slaves for their times, computes average (excluding outliers), sends each node its required adjustment. No external time source needed—internal consistency only.

questions.question: Why might a distributed database need synchronized clocks?

options.text: To order transactions, determine causality, and implement consistency guarantees
Clocks are not needed in databases

questions.explanation: Databases use timestamps for: transaction ordering (snapshot isolation), conflict resolution (last-write-wins), TTL/expiration, audit logs. Poor synchronization can cause anomalies or incorrect ordering.

questions.question: What is the difference between clock synchronization and logical clocks?

options.text: Clock sync aligns physical time; logical clocks track causality without physical time

questions.explanation: Clock synchronization: align wall-clock time across nodes (NTP, GPS). Logical clocks (Lamport, Vector): track event ordering through message passing, no physical time needed. Different tools for different problems.

questions.question: What is PTP (Precision Time Protocol) and when is it used?

options.text: A high-precision time sync protocol achieving sub-microsecond accuracy, used in finance and telecom

questions.explanation: PTP (IEEE 1588) achieves nanosecond-level accuracy using hardware timestamping. Used in: high-frequency trading, telecom, industrial automation. More complex and expensive than NTP.

questions.question: A distributed system uses timestamps for conflict resolution. Clocks are synchronized to within 100ms. What's a potential issue?

options.text: Events within 100ms window may be ordered incorrectly, causing wrong conflict resolution

questions.explanation: With 100ms uncertainty, two events 50ms apart might be ordered wrong. Last-write-wins could pick the wrong write. Solutions: larger uncertainty windows, logical clocks, or hybrid approaches.
